questions.prompt: For a differentiable objective and a convex feasible set, the variational inequality at a candidate \(x^\star\) says that
questions.explanation: Every feasible step has to look uphill, or flat, to first order, so the gradient pairs nonnegatively with \(x - x^\star\). The opposite sign is the obtuse-angle test for a projection, not this inequality. A boundary minimizer can have a nonzero gradient that points out of the set. Points outside the set are not feasible steps, so the inequality is not a claim about them.

options: \(\nabla f(x^\star)^T (x - x^\star) \ge 0\) for every feasible \(x\)

\(\nabla f(x^\star) = 0\), even when \(x^\star\) lies on the boundary
\(\nabla f(x^\star)^T (x - x^\star) \ge 0\) for every \(x\) outside the set

questions.prompt: Minimize \(\tfrac12 (t - 5)^2\) on the interval \([-1,\ 2]\). At the candidate \(t = 2\), what is the gradient's product with the feasible step from \(2\) to \(0\)?
questions.explanation: The gradient of \(\tfrac12 (t - 5)^2\) is \(t - 5\). At \(t = 2\) it equals \(-3\). The step from \(2\) to \(0\) is \(-2\). The product is \((-3)(-2) = 6\). Reporting \(-3\) is the gradient. Reporting \(-6\) flips the sign of the inequality. Reporting \(2\) is the candidate, not the product. The positive product is what the variational inequality asks for along this particular step.

questions.prompt: If the variational inequality holds at a point in the interior of the convex set, then
questions.explanation: An interior point has a small ball of feasible steps. A nonnegative pairing in a direction and in its opposite forces each pairing to be zero, so the gradient is zero. That is the unconstrained stationarity test. The point is feasible by the interior assumption. Convexity of the objective is not required for this conclusion.

the point is infeasible

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that checks the variational inequality at one candidate on a convex polygon. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The dot products use the gradient, so the gradient comes first. The comparisons use those products, so they come after the products are formed. The accept-or-reject decision uses the comparisons. A linear function on a polygon attains its minimum at a vertex, so the products at the vertices decide the inequality for every feasible point. Checking a single edge before the gradient exists is not a reordering of these steps.

questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: Evaluate the gradient at the candidate.
Using that gradient, form its dot product with the vector from the candidate to each vertex.
Compare each of those dot products with zero.
Accept the candidate only when every one of those dot products is nonnegative.

questions.prompt: Minimize the objective \(x\) on the unit square \([0,\ 1] \times [0,\ 1]\). Which points satisfy the variational inequality?
questions.explanation:
The gradient is \((1,\ 0)\). At a feasible point \(p\), the product with \(x - p\) is the first coordinate of \(x - p\).
• At \((0,\ 0)\), \((0,\ 1)\), and \((0,\ 1/2)\) that difference of first coordinates is nonnegative everywhere in the square, because every feasible first coordinate is at least \(0\).
• At \((1,\ 1/5)\) the step back to \((0,\ 1/5)\) has product \(-1\).
• At \((2/5,\ 2/5)\) the step back to \((0,\ 2/5)\) has product \(-2/5\).
The whole left edge is optimal for this linear objective. The other two points are not.

questions.prompt: On the interval from \(0\) to \(a\), with the objective \(\tfrac12 (t - b)^2\), the candidate is the right endpoint \(t = a\). The product of the gradient at \(a\) with the step from \(a\) to \(0\) equals
questions.explanation: The gradient of \(\tfrac12 (t - b)^2\) is \(t - b\). At \(t = a\) it equals \(a - b\). The step from \(a\) to \(0\) is \(-a\). The product is \((a - b)(-a) = a(b - a)\). Both names appear. Using \(a - b\) alone drops the step. Using \(b - a\) alone drops the factor from the step length. Adding \(a + b\) mixes the endpoint with the unconstrained minimizer.

questions.prompt: A note checks \(t = 4\) for \(\min (t - 1)^2\) on \([0,\ 4]\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The set and the candidate are as stated. The derivative of \((t - 1)^2\) is \(2(t - 1)\), so the value at \(4\) is \(6\). Feasible steps from the right endpoint point left, so \(t - 4 \le 0\). The product of a positive gradient with a negative step is negative, not positive. The inequality fails, and the minimizer of this convex objective is the left side of the unconstrained minimizer, at \(t = 1\).

steps: The feasible set is \([0,\ 4]\) and the candidate is the right endpoint \(4\).
For every feasible \(t\), the step \(t - 4\) is less than or equal to \(0\).
The product \(6(t - 4)\) is positive for every \(t < 4\), so the variational inequality holds.
reasons: The product \(6(t - 4)\) is negative for \(t < 4\), so the variational inequality does not hold.
The gradient of \((t - 1)^2\) at \(4\) is not \(6\).
The endpoint \(4\) is outside the interval.

questions.prompt: On the interval \([-2,\ 2]\), the objective \(-t^2\) has gradient zero at \(t = 0\). How much larger is the objective at \(0\) than at \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The values are \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f(2) = -4\), so the difference is \(4\). The variational inequality holds at \(0\) because the gradient is zero, but \(2\) is feasible and better. A zero gradient is not a certificate of a minimum when the objective is not convex. Reporting \(-4\) is the endpoint value, not the difference. Reporting \(0\) would be the value at the stationary point.

questions.prompt: When the objective is convex and the feasible set is convex, the variational inequality is
questions.explanation: Convexity puts \(f(x)\) above \(f(x^\star) + \nabla f(x^\star)^T (x - x^\star)\). If every feasible pairing is nonnegative, no feasible point can undercut \(f(x^\star)\). For a convex objective the certificate is global, not merely local. A convex function does not satisfy the inequality at a maximizer unless the function is flat. The Hessian test is a different, second-order statement.

options: sufficient for a local minimizer that need not be global
the same statement as a positive definite Hessian
sufficient for a global minimizer, because the graph stays above its tangent
only necessary, and a convex objective can satisfy it at a maximizer

questions.prompt: A local minimizer of a differentiable objective over a convex set
questions.explanation: Necessity uses the set's convexity and differentiability: a descent step would contradict a local minimum. Convexity of the objective is what upgrades the inequality from necessary to sufficient. A smooth objective on a disk can be minimized at an interior point or at a non-vertex boundary point. A boundary minimizer can have a nonzero gradient pointing out of the set.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x - 1)^2 + (y - 4)^2\) on the box \([0,\ 3] \times [0,\ 2]\). At the candidate \((1,\ 2)\), what is the gradient's product with the step from \((1,\ 2)\) to \((0,\ 0)\)?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \((2(x - 1),\ 2(y - 4))\). At \((1,\ 2)\) it equals \((0,\ -4)\). The step to \((0,\ 0)\) is \((-1,\ -2)\). The product is \((-4)(-2) = 8\). The first coordinate does not contribute. Reporting \(-8\) flips the sign. Reporting \(4\) is the absolute value of one gradient entry. The candidate is the point of the box closest to the unconstrained minimizer \((1,\ 4)\), which sits above the box.

questions.prompt: For a differentiable objective that is not convex, a feasible point that satisfies the variational inequality
questions.explanation: The inequality is necessary for a local minimum, but it is not sufficient without convexity. The objective \(-t^2\) on an interval has a zero gradient at an interior maximum, so the inequality holds and the point is not a minimizer. Global optimality needs the tangent lower bound that convexity supplies. A zero gradient is allowed, and the point need not be a vertex.
